claims.text: The starting protective coating has a mixed FCC/BCC microstructure produced by thermal spray or cladding.
Creep resistance under continuous loading is primarily controlled by heterogeneous boundaries between FCC and BCC regions.
Hindering dislocation motion reduces the creep-deformation rate.
Thermal spray or cladding produces a more heterogeneous FCC/BCC interface distribution than an alternative homogeneous deposition technique.
The governing structural mediator is the distribution of heterogeneous interfaces between FCC and BCC phases.
Phase boundaries generated by thermal spray or cladding obstruct both dislocation glide and dislocation climb.
Impeded dislocation glide and climb under sustained loading lower the creep strain rate relative to a uniform microstructure.
Thermal-sprayed or clad coatings will have a significantly lower creep strain rate than coatings with a homogeneous phase structure.
Thermal-sprayed or clad coatings will undergo less progressive plastic deformation than homogeneous coatings.
A homogeneous reference coating is expected to exhibit greater creep deformation under the same stress and temperature conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies under sustained high stress and elevated temperature below phase-transformation thresholds.
The mechanism is not expected to govern when phase transformations, oxidation, or other degradation mechanisms dominate.
Interface density should correlate with improved creep resistance.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate or a correlation between phase-boundary distribution and creep resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
